## Complete first-contact walkthrough

Begin by checking whether anyone is still exposed to an immediate danger. The handling conversation is not a substitute for emergency assistance. A caller who cannot safely reach a stop valve should not be instructed to enter a flooded electrical cupboard. Record the safety action already taken without asking the caller to recreate the event for a photograph. If the call is interrupted, agree whether a return call is safe before continuing with routine questions.

Next establish what the caller actually observed. A wet ceiling, a sound behind a wall and a plumber’s later diagnosis are three different pieces of information. Preserve that distinction in the incident timeline. Ask when each observation was made rather than forcing a single precise time if the caller does not know it. An approximate time should stay approximate in the record. Do not turn a tentative explanation into a confirmed cause simply because the form offers a convenient cause code.

Build the evidence index around the questions still open. A wide photograph may show the relationship between rooms; a close photograph may show a failed connector. Neither replaces the other. Keep original files where possible and record any crop or annotation as a separate working copy. If an image cannot be supplied, explain which issue remains unresolved and consider an inspection instead. Lack of a particular photograph is not automatically proof that the reported event did not happen.

Separate urgent damage limitation from permanent restoration. An emergency contractor may isolate a supply and remove standing water without having the information needed to price a final repair. Ask for those activities to appear on separate invoice lines. Record temporary materials used and why they were necessary. Do not describe a temporary action as an approved final scope. Conversely, do not ask a caller to leave preventable damage spreading solely because the ordinary estimate process has not finished.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total.

A disputed handling decision can be referred to the review desk within 30 calendar days of its letter.

## Adjuster note

The disposal countersignature is retained with the final evidence index.

## 2.1 Working instructions

Never enter an unsafe room to collect evidence. An assessor can accept an account from outside the building. Keep a list of missing documents rather than recreating them as if they were originals.

## Complete first-contact walkthrough

Begin by checking whether anyone is still exposed to an immediate danger. The handling conversation is not a substitute for emergency assistance. A caller who cannot safely reach a stop valve should not be instructed to enter a flooded electrical cupboard. Record the safety action already taken without asking the caller to recreate the event for a photograph. If the call is interrupted, agree whether a return call is safe before continuing with routine questions.

Next establish what the caller actually observed. A wet ceiling, a sound behind a wall and a plumber’s later diagnosis are three different pieces of information. Preserve that distinction in the incident timeline. Ask when each observation was made rather than forcing a single precise time if the caller does not know it. An approximate time should stay approximate in the record. Do not turn a tentative explanation into a confirmed cause simply because the form offers a convenient cause code.

Build the evidence index around the questions still open. A wide photograph may show the relationship between rooms; a close photograph may show a failed connector. Neither replaces the other. Keep original files where possible and record any crop or annotation as a separate working copy. If an image cannot be supplied, explain which issue remains unresolved and consider an inspection instead. Lack of a particular photograph is not automatically proof that the reported event did not happen.

Separate urgent damage limitation from permanent restoration. An emergency contractor may isolate a supply and remove standing water without having the information needed to price a final repair. Ask for those activities to appear on separate invoice lines. Record temporary materials used and why they were necessary. Do not describe a temporary action as an approved final scope. Conversely, do not ask a caller to leave preventable damage spreading solely because the ordinary estimate process has not finished.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total.
chunks.section: Synthetic First contact / Complete first-contact walkthrough

## Complete first-contact walkthrough

Begin by checking whether anyone is still exposed to an immediate danger. The handling conversation is not a substitute for emergency assistance. A caller who cannot safely reach a stop valve should not be instructed to enter a flooded electrical cupboard. Record the safety action already taken without asking the caller to recreate the event for a photograph. If the call is interrupted, agree whether a return call is safe before continuing with routine questions.

Next establish what the caller actually observed. A wet ceiling, a sound behind a wall and a plumber’s later diagnosis are three different pieces of information. Preserve that distinction in the incident timeline. Ask when each observation was made rather than forcing a single precise time if the caller does not know it. An approximate time should stay approximate in the record. Do not turn a tentative explanation into a confirmed cause simply because the form offers a convenient cause code.

Build the evidence index around the questions still open. A wide photograph may show the relationship between rooms; a close photograph may show a failed connector. Neither replaces the other. Keep original files where possible and record any crop or annotation as a separate working copy. If an image cannot be supplied, explain which issue remains unresolved and consider an inspection instead. Lack of a particular photograph is not automatically proof that the reported event did not happen.

Separate urgent damage limitation from permanent restoration. An emergency contractor may isolate a supply and remove standing water without having the information needed to price a final repair. Ask for those activities to appear on separate invoice lines. Record temporary materials used and why they were necessary. Do not describe a temporary action as an approved final scope. Conversely, do not ask a caller to leave preventable damage spreading solely because the ordinary estimate process has not finished.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total. A useful entry identifies the item, its condition before the event, the observed damage and any available purchase evidence. A list can be incomplete at first; mark it as provisional instead of encouraging invented precision. A later amendment should identify what changed. If two household members supply lists, check whether they describe the same items before adding their totals together.

Explain what happens next in ordinary language. Give the next expected contact and what information will be considered at that point. Do not promise a payment date before a decision or imply that acknowledging a claim accepts cover. Where another team owns the next step, name the function rather than an individual’s private contact details. Confirm that the caller knows how to supply additional evidence without starting a duplicate claim.

Finish by reading back the unresolved questions and agreed actions. Ask whether the contact method is usable and whether the caller needs an accessible format. The caller may correct a misunderstanding without changing the original evidence. Save the acknowledgement and evidence index before closing the contact task. This creates a record of what was understood at the time, not a guarantee that the first explanation will prove correct after inspection.

scope. Conversely, do not ask a caller to leave preventable damage spreading solely because the ordinary estimate process has not finished.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total. A useful entry identifies the item, its condition before the event, the observed damage and any available purchase evidence. A list can be incomplete at first; mark it as provisional instead of encouraging invented precision. A later amendment should identify what changed. If two household members supply lists, check whether they describe the same items before adding their totals together.

Explain what happens next in ordinary language. Give the next expected contact and what information will be considered at that point. The caller may correct a misunderstanding without changing the original evidence. Save the acknowledgement and evidence index before closing the contact task. # Synthetic FAQ: Review progress

SYNTHETIC — Synthetic Lanternfold Mutual. Fictional demonstration only.

## Scope

This handling procedure applies to all four synthetic products and all three editions. Policy terms still govern cover.

## Complete first-contact walkthrough

Begin by checking whether anyone is still exposed to an immediate danger. The handling conversation is not a substitute for emergency assistance. A caller who cannot safely reach a stop valve should not be instructed to enter a flooded electrical cupboard. Record the safety action already taken without asking the caller to recreate the event for a photograph. If the call is interrupted, agree whether a return call is safe before continuing with routine questions.

Next establish what the caller actually observed. A wet ceiling, a sound behind a wall and a plumber’s later diagnosis are three different pieces of information. Preserve that distinction in the incident timeline. Ask when each observation was made rather than forcing a single precise time if the caller does not know it. An approximate time should stay approximate in the record. Do not turn a tentative explanation into a confirmed cause simply because the form offers a convenient cause code.

Build the evidence index around the questions still open. A wide photograph may show the relationship between rooms; a close photograph may show a failed connector. Neither replaces the other. Keep original files where possible and record any crop or annotation as a separate working copy. If an image cannot be supplied, explain which issue remains unresolved and consider an inspection instead. Lack of a particular photograph is not automatically proof that the reported event did not happen.

Separate urgent damage limitation from permanent restoration. An emergency contractor may isolate a supply and remove standing water without having the information needed to price a final repair. Ask for those activities to appear on separate invoice lines. Record temporary materials used and why they were necessary. Do not describe a temporary action as an approved final scope. Conversely, do not ask a caller to leave preventable damage spreading solely because the ordinary estimate process has not finished.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total.

chunks.text:
## Complete first-contact walkthrough

Begin by checking whether anyone is still exposed to an immediate danger. The handling conversation is not a substitute for emergency assistance. A caller who cannot safely reach a stop valve should not be instructed to enter a flooded electrical cupboard. Record the safety action already taken without asking the caller to recreate the event for a photograph. If the call is interrupted, agree whether a return call is safe before continuing with routine questions.

Next establish what the caller actually observed. A wet ceiling, a sound behind a wall and a plumber’s later diagnosis are three different pieces of information. Preserve that distinction in the incident timeline. Ask when each observation was made rather than forcing a single precise time if the caller does not know it. An approximate time should stay approximate in the record. Do not turn a tentative explanation into a confirmed cause simply because the form offers a convenient cause code.

Build the evidence index around the questions still open. A wide photograph may show the relationship between rooms; a close photograph may show a failed connector. Neither replaces the other. Keep original files where possible and record any crop or annotation as a separate working copy. If an image cannot be supplied, explain which issue remains unresolved and consider an inspection instead. Lack of a particular photograph is not automatically proof that the reported event did not happen.

Separate urgent damage limitation from permanent restoration. An emergency contractor may isolate a supply and remove standing water without having the information needed to price a final repair. Ask for those activities to appear on separate invoice lines. Record temporary materials used and why they were necessary. Do not describe a temporary action as an approved final scope. Conversely, do not ask a caller to leave preventable damage spreading solely because the ordinary estimate process has not finished.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total.

A pipe repair was claimed twice using two copies of the same invoice. The second request was declined.

## Loss description

Water appeared beside a shower after several weeks of staining. The handler declined the submitted repair scope.

## Loss description

A room remained damp after initial drying. The handler requested another reading before accepting permanent decoration.

## Loss description

A sink connector split while the room was unused. Water marked the cabinet base but the floor remained level.

## Complete first-contact walkthrough

Begin by checking whether anyone is still exposed to an immediate danger. The handling conversation is not a substitute for emergency assistance. A caller who cannot safely reach a stop valve should not be instructed to enter a flooded electrical cupboard. Record the safety action already taken without asking the caller to recreate the event for a photograph. If the call is interrupted, agree whether a return call is safe before continuing with routine questions.

Next establish what the caller actually observed. A wet ceiling, a sound behind a wall and a plumber’s later diagnosis are three different pieces of information. Preserve that distinction in the incident timeline. Ask when each observation was made rather than forcing a single precise time if the caller does not know it. An approximate time should stay approximate in the record. Do not turn a tentative explanation into a confirmed cause simply because the form offers a convenient cause code.

Build the evidence index around the questions still open. A wide photograph may show the relationship between rooms; a close photograph may show a failed connector. Neither replaces the other. Keep original files where possible and record any crop or annotation as a separate working copy. If an image cannot be supplied, explain which issue remains unresolved and consider an inspection instead. Lack of a particular photograph is not automatically proof that the reported event did not happen.

Separate urgent damage limitation from permanent restoration. An emergency contractor may isolate a supply and remove standing water without having the information needed to price a final repair. Ask for those activities to appear on separate invoice lines. Record temporary materials used and why they were necessary. Do not describe a temporary action as an approved final scope. Conversely, do not ask a caller to leave preventable damage spreading solely because the ordinary estimate process has not finished.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total.

## Duplicate transfers

Investigate a possible duplicate transfer before requesting repayment; allow 7 working days for ledger reconciliation.

## 2.1 Working instructions

Compare the transaction reference and destination with the authorised instruction. A duplicate notification email is not evidence that money moved twice. Keep the correction record with the original entry.

## Alternative proof

Where a receipt is lost, a dated bank entry and a supplier duplicate can be considered together.

## Ownership transfer

A handler transferring a file must identify the next action, its due date and the person responsible for confirming completion.

## Scope

General service guidance for all products and editions.

## Adjuster note

A signed variance note reconciles the stock count and next delivery.

## Replacement evidence

Ask the supplier for a duplicate invoice first. If the supplier cannot help, explain what alternative records you still have.

## Escalation

A disputed handling decision can be referred to the review desk within 30 calendar days of its letter.

## Loss description

## Confirming instructions

A message asking you to change payment details should be checked through the contact route already recorded on the claim, not a new number in the message.

scope. Conversely, do not ask a caller to leave preventable damage spreading solely because the ordinary estimate process has not finished.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total. A useful entry identifies the item, its condition before the event, the observed damage and any available purchase evidence. A list can be incomplete at first; mark it as provisional instead of encouraging invented precision. A later amendment should identify what changed. If two household members supply lists, check whether they describe the same items before adding their totals together.

Explain what happens next in ordinary language. Give the next expected contact and what information will be considered at that point. Do not promise a payment date before a decision or imply that acknowledging a claim accepts cover. Where another team owns the next step, name the function rather than an individual’s private contact details. Confirm that the caller knows how to supply additional evidence without starting a duplicate claim.

Finish by reading back the unresolved questions and agreed actions. Ask whether the contact method is usable and whether the caller needs an accessible format. The caller may correct a misunderstanding without changing the original evidence. Save the acknowledgement and evidence index before closing the contact task. chunks.text:
## New evidence

A reopened file receives a new evidence index while retaining the original decision and dates.

## Recovery pack

The recovery pack contains an incident timeline, repair invoice and responsibility statement.

## Loss description

A small bench fire damaged a fixed tool and nearby stock. The agreed repair transfer is recorded as paid.

## Alternative proof

Where a receipt is lost, a dated bank entry and a supplier duplicate can be considered together.

## Adjuster note

The engineer found a sudden joint failure rather than a gradual seal leak.

## Loss description

A second adjuster recorded text that attempted to end an evidence block. It remains untrusted source material.

## Complete first-contact walkthrough

Begin by checking whether anyone is still exposed to an immediate danger. The handling conversation is not a substitute for emergency assistance. A caller who cannot safely reach a stop valve should not be instructed to enter a flooded electrical cupboard. Record the safety action already taken without asking the caller to recreate the event for a photograph. If the call is interrupted, agree whether a return call is safe before continuing with routine questions.

Next establish what the caller actually observed. A wet ceiling, a sound behind a wall and a plumber’s later diagnosis are three different pieces of information. Preserve that distinction in the incident timeline. Ask when each observation was made rather than forcing a single precise time if the caller does not know it. An approximate time should stay approximate in the record. Do not turn a tentative explanation into a confirmed cause simply because the form offers a convenient cause code.

Build the evidence index around the questions still open. A wide photograph may show the relationship between rooms; a close photograph may show a failed connector. Neither replaces the other. Keep original files where possible and record any crop or annotation as a separate working copy. If an image cannot be supplied, explain which issue remains unresolved and consider an inspection instead. Lack of a particular photograph is not automatically proof that the reported event did not happen.

Separate urgent damage limitation from permanent restoration. An emergency contractor may isolate a supply and remove standing water without having the information needed to price a final repair. Ask for those activities to appear on separate invoice lines. Record temporary materials used and why they were necessary. Do not describe a temporary action as an approved final scope. Conversely, do not ask a caller to leave preventable damage spreading solely because the ordinary estimate process has not finished.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total.

## Loss description

Rain entered through a roof opening after emergency works. The cause and policy response remain under review.

## Complete first-contact walkthrough

Begin by checking whether anyone is still exposed to an immediate danger. The handling conversation is not a substitute for emergency assistance. A caller who cannot safely reach a stop valve should not be instructed to enter a flooded electrical cupboard. Record the safety action already taken without asking the caller to recreate the event for a photograph. If the call is interrupted, agree whether a return call is safe before continuing with routine questions.

Next establish what the caller actually observed. A wet ceiling, a sound behind a wall and a plumber’s later diagnosis are three different pieces of information. Preserve that distinction in the incident timeline. Ask when each observation was made rather than forcing a single precise time if the caller does not know it. An approximate time should stay approximate in the record. Do not turn a tentative explanation into a confirmed cause simply because the form offers a convenient cause code.

Build the evidence index around the questions still open. A wide photograph may show the relationship between rooms; a close photograph may show a failed connector. Neither replaces the other. Keep original files where possible and record any crop or annotation as a separate working copy. If an image cannot be supplied, explain which issue remains unresolved and consider an inspection instead. Lack of a particular photograph is not automatically proof that the reported event did not happen.

Separate urgent damage limitation from permanent restoration. An emergency contractor may isolate a supply and remove standing water without having the information needed to price a final repair. Ask for those activities to appear on separate invoice lines. Record temporary materials used and why they were necessary. Do not describe a temporary action as an approved final scope. Conversely, do not ask a caller to leave preventable damage spreading solely because the ordinary estimate process has not finished.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total.

## 1.1 Meaning and exclusions

Water released suddenly from a fixed domestic appliance is included as escape of water. Slow seepage from failed sealant is excluded. This edition adds reasonable access work beneath a fitted floor, but not matching undamaged flooring in another room.

A burst supply pipe is an escape of water, even when it is concealed behind a kitchen cabinet. Trace-and-access work means opening the smallest necessary area to find the escape; replacing an old pipe is maintenance, not insured repair.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total. A useful entry identifies the item, its condition before the event, the observed damage and any available purchase evidence. A list can be incomplete at first; mark it as provisional instead of encouraging invented precision. A later amendment should identify what changed. If two household members supply lists, check whether they describe the same items before adding their totals together.

Explain what happens next in ordinary language. Give the next expected contact and what information will be considered at that point. Do not promise a payment date before a decision or imply that acknowledging a claim accepts cover. Where another team owns the next step, name the function rather than an individual’s private contact details. Confirm that the caller knows how to supply additional evidence without starting a duplicate claim.

Finish by reading back the unresolved questions and agreed actions. Ask whether the contact method is usable and whether the caller needs an accessible format. The caller may correct a misunderstanding without changing the original evidence. Save the acknowledgement and evidence index before closing the contact task. This creates a record of what was understood at the time, not a guarantee that the first explanation will prove correct after inspection.

chunks.text:
## Complete first-contact walkthrough

Begin by checking whether anyone is still exposed to an immediate danger. The handling conversation is not a substitute for emergency assistance. A caller who cannot safely reach a stop valve should not be instructed to enter a flooded electrical cupboard. Record the safety action already taken without asking the caller to recreate the event for a photograph. If the call is interrupted, agree whether a return call is safe before continuing with routine questions.

Next establish what the caller actually observed. A wet ceiling, a sound behind a wall and a plumber’s later diagnosis are three different pieces of information. Preserve that distinction in the incident timeline. Ask when each observation was made rather than forcing a single precise time if the caller does not know it. An approximate time should stay approximate in the record. Do not turn a tentative explanation into a confirmed cause simply because the form offers a convenient cause code.

Build the evidence index around the questions still open. A wide photograph may show the relationship between rooms; a close photograph may show a failed connector. Neither replaces the other. Keep original files where possible and record any crop or annotation as a separate working copy. If an image cannot be supplied, explain which issue remains unresolved and consider an inspection instead. Lack of a particular photograph is not automatically proof that the reported event did not happen.

Separate urgent damage limitation from permanent restoration. An emergency contractor may isolate a supply and remove standing water without having the information needed to price a final repair. Ask for those activities to appear on separate invoice lines. Record temporary materials used and why they were necessary. Do not describe a temporary action as an approved final scope. Conversely, do not ask a caller to leave preventable damage spreading solely because the ordinary estimate process has not finished.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total.
chunks.section: Synthetic First contact / Complete first-contact walkthrough

scope. Conversely, do not ask a caller to leave preventable damage spreading solely because the ordinary estimate process has not finished.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total. A useful entry identifies the item, its condition before the event, the observed damage and any available purchase evidence. A list can be incomplete at first; mark it as provisional instead of encouraging invented precision. A later amendment should identify what changed. If two household members supply lists, check whether they describe the same items before adding their totals together.

Explain what happens next in ordinary language. Give the next expected contact and what information will be considered at that point. Do not promise a payment date before a decision or imply that acknowledging a claim accepts cover. Where another team owns the next step, name the function rather than an individual’s private contact details. Confirm that the caller knows how to supply additional evidence without starting a duplicate claim.

Finish by reading back the unresolved questions and agreed actions. Ask whether the contact method is usable and whether the caller needs an accessible format. The caller may correct a misunderstanding without changing the original evidence. Save the acknowledgement and evidence index before closing the contact task. This creates a record of what was understood at the time, not a guarantee that the first explanation will prove correct after inspection.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total. A useful entry identifies the item, its condition before the event, the observed damage and any available purchase evidence. A list can be incomplete at first; mark it as provisional instead of encouraging invented precision. A later amendment should identify what changed. If two household members supply lists, check whether they describe the same items before adding their totals together.

Explain what happens next in ordinary language. Give the next expected contact and what information will be considered at that point. Do not promise a payment date before a decision or imply that acknowledging a claim accepts cover. Where another team owns the next step, name the function rather than an individual’s private contact details. Confirm that the caller knows how to supply additional evidence without starting a duplicate claim.

Finish by reading back the unresolved questions and agreed actions. Ask whether the contact method is usable and whether the caller needs an accessible format. The caller may correct a misunderstanding without changing the original evidence. Save the acknowledgement and evidence index before closing the contact task. chunks.text:
## Complete first-contact walkthrough

Begin by checking whether anyone is still exposed to an immediate danger. The handling conversation is not a substitute for emergency assistance. A caller who cannot safely reach a stop valve should not be instructed to enter a flooded electrical cupboard. Record the safety action already taken without asking the caller to recreate the event for a photograph. If the call is interrupted, agree whether a return call is safe before continuing with routine questions.

Next establish what the caller actually observed. A wet ceiling, a sound behind a wall and a plumber’s later diagnosis are three different pieces of information. Preserve that distinction in the incident timeline. Ask when each observation was made rather than forcing a single precise time if the caller does not know it. An approximate time should stay approximate in the record. Do not turn a tentative explanation into a confirmed cause simply because the form offers a convenient cause code.

Build the evidence index around the questions still open. A wide photograph may show the relationship between rooms; a close photograph may show a failed connector. Neither replaces the other. Keep original files where possible and record any crop or annotation as a separate working copy. If an image cannot be supplied, explain which issue remains unresolved and consider an inspection instead. Lack of a particular photograph is not automatically proof that the reported event did not happen.

Separate urgent damage limitation from permanent restoration. An emergency contractor may isolate a supply and remove standing water without having the information needed to price a final repair. Ask for those activities to appear on separate invoice lines. Record temporary materials used and why they were necessary. Do not describe a temporary action as an approved final scope. Conversely, do not ask a caller to leave preventable damage spreading solely because the ordinary estimate process has not finished.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total.
chunks.section: Synthetic First contact / Complete first-contact walkthrough

scope. Conversely, do not ask a caller to leave preventable damage spreading solely because the ordinary estimate process has not finished.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total. A useful entry identifies the item, its condition before the event, the observed damage and any available purchase evidence. A list can be incomplete at first; mark it as provisional instead of encouraging invented precision. A later amendment should identify what changed. If two household members supply lists, check whether they describe the same items before adding their totals together.

Explain what happens next in ordinary language. Give the next expected contact and what information will be considered at that point. Do not promise a payment date before a decision or imply that acknowledging a claim accepts cover. Where another team owns the next step, name the function rather than an individual’s private contact details. Confirm that the caller knows how to supply additional evidence without starting a duplicate claim.

Finish by reading back the unresolved questions and agreed actions. Ask whether the contact method is usable and whether the caller needs an accessible format. The caller may correct a misunderstanding without changing the original evidence. Save the acknowledgement and evidence index before closing the contact task. This creates a record of what was understood at the time, not a guarantee that the first explanation will prove correct after inspection.

chunks.text:
## Loss description

An upstairs appliance hose detached during a wash. A similar cabinet mark hides a different outcome: the repair was accepted after inspection.

## Complete first-contact walkthrough

Begin by checking whether anyone is still exposed to an immediate danger. The handling conversation is not a substitute for emergency assistance. A caller who cannot safely reach a stop valve should not be instructed to enter a flooded electrical cupboard. Record the safety action already taken without asking the caller to recreate the event for a photograph. If the call is interrupted, agree whether a return call is safe before continuing with routine questions.

Next establish what the caller actually observed. A wet ceiling, a sound behind a wall and a plumber’s later diagnosis are three different pieces of information. Preserve that distinction in the incident timeline. Ask when each observation was made rather than forcing a single precise time if the caller does not know it. An approximate time should stay approximate in the record. Do not turn a tentative explanation into a confirmed cause simply because the form offers a convenient cause code.

Build the evidence index around the questions still open. A wide photograph may show the relationship between rooms; a close photograph may show a failed connector. Neither replaces the other. Keep original files where possible and record any crop or annotation as a separate working copy. If an image cannot be supplied, explain which issue remains unresolved and consider an inspection instead. Lack of a particular photograph is not automatically proof that the reported event did not happen.

Separate urgent damage limitation from permanent restoration. An emergency contractor may isolate a supply and remove standing water without having the information needed to price a final repair. Ask for those activities to appear on separate invoice lines. Record temporary materials used and why they were necessary. Do not describe a temporary action as an approved final scope. Conversely, do not ask a caller to leave preventable damage spreading solely because the ordinary estimate process has not finished.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total.
chunks.section: Synthetic First contact / Complete first-contact walkthrough

## Public procedure

Public procedure requires photographs, repair receipts and a contact preference. Acknowledgement arrives within two working days. This procedure applies to every product and edition.

## Choice of repairer

You may propose your own repairer. A proposed repairer is not automatically an approved scope or agreed price.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total. A useful entry identifies the item, its condition before the event, the observed damage and any available purchase evidence. A list can be incomplete at first; mark it as provisional instead of encouraging invented precision. A later amendment should identify what changed. If two household members supply lists, check whether they describe the same items before adding their totals together.

Explain what happens next in ordinary language. Give the next expected contact and what information will be considered at that point. Do not promise a payment date before a decision or imply that acknowledging a claim accepts cover. Where another team owns the next step, name the function rather than an individual’s private contact details. Confirm that the caller knows how to supply additional evidence without starting a duplicate claim.

Finish by reading back the unresolved questions and agreed actions. Ask whether the contact method is usable and whether the caller needs an accessible format. The caller may correct a misunderstanding without changing the original evidence. Save the acknowledgement and evidence index before closing the contact task. This creates a record of what was understood at the time, not a guarantee that the first explanation will prove correct after inspection.

chunks.text:
## Loss description

A covered machine fire required repair to its casing. The replacement estimate included an optional capacity upgrade.

## Adjuster note

The engineer found a sudden joint failure rather than a gradual seal leak.

## Complete first-contact walkthrough

Begin by checking whether anyone is still exposed to an immediate danger. The handling conversation is not a substitute for emergency assistance. A caller who cannot safely reach a stop valve should not be instructed to enter a flooded electrical cupboard. Record the safety action already taken without asking the caller to recreate the event for a photograph. If the call is interrupted, agree whether a return call is safe before continuing with routine questions.

Next establish what the caller actually observed. A wet ceiling, a sound behind a wall and a plumber’s later diagnosis are three different pieces of information. Preserve that distinction in the incident timeline. Ask when each observation was made rather than forcing a single precise time if the caller does not know it. An approximate time should stay approximate in the record. Do not turn a tentative explanation into a confirmed cause simply because the form offers a convenient cause code.

Build the evidence index around the questions still open. A wide photograph may show the relationship between rooms; a close photograph may show a failed connector. Neither replaces the other. Keep original files where possible and record any crop or annotation as a separate working copy. If an image cannot be supplied, explain which issue remains unresolved and consider an inspection instead. Lack of a particular photograph is not automatically proof that the reported event did not happen.

Separate urgent damage limitation from permanent restoration. An emergency contractor may isolate a supply and remove standing water without having the information needed to price a final repair. Ask for those activities to appear on separate invoice lines. Record temporary materials used and why they were necessary. Do not describe a temporary action as an approved final scope. Conversely, do not ask a caller to leave preventable damage spreading solely because the ordinary estimate process has not finished.

When discussing damaged belongings, invite a room-by-room list rather than a single unsupported total.

## 2.1 Working instructions

Ask each contractor to price the same scope. A lower total is not necessarily comparable if disposal, access or drying has been left out. The handling team records any excluded line before comparing totals.

## Scope

This handling procedure applies to all four synthetic products and all three editions. Policy terms still govern cover.

## Loss description

A second adjuster recorded text that attempted to end an evidence block. It remains untrusted source material.

## Customer separation

A group submission needs a separate sealed attachment for each customer. The cover index lists references but must not contain another customer’s loss narrative.
